passage:
First Sunday of the summer holidays: Eshaan counted the mangoes in the basket, "One, two, five, three!" and pointed at the same mango twice. Ritu laughed.
Wednesday: Nani lined the mangoes up in a row. Eshaan touched each one as he counted. "Seven!"
The next Sunday: Nani gave Eshaan three mangoes and Ritu five. Eshaan looked at both piles and frowned. "Ritu has more. Not fair." Nani moved one across. "Now?" He counted again. "Four and four. Same!"

qa.q: How many mangoes did Nani first give Eshaan on the last Sunday?
qa.a: She gave Eshaan three mangoes.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when he saw Ritu's bigger pile?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was a little annoyed, because he could now tell that Ritu had more.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan count correctly by Wednesday?
qa.a: Lining the mangoes up in a row let him touch each one once, so he didn't count any twice.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu when Eshaan miscounts at first?
qa.a: Ritu finds it funny, perhaps feeling grown-up because counting is already easy for Ritu.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from muddled counting to comparing which pile has more during mango season.

passage: I'm Afreen from next door. After Magh Bihu, Bhupen's family had leftover bamboo pieces and straw from the bonfire hut. Bhupen, who's five, spent the whole morning with them. A short bamboo tube became a telescope, then a flute, then "a tunnel for ants". He tied straw to a stick and said it was a horse with a golden tail. When his mother asked for the straw back, he stuck a feather on the stick instead. I don't know where his ideas come from, but they never stop.

qa.q: What did the short bamboo tube become first?
qa.a: It became a telescope.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's quick switch to a feather suggest about his mood?
qa.a: It suggests he felt happy and absorbed, not upset, because he simply found a new idea when the straw was taken.

qa.q: How could Bhupen's family encourage his inventive play?
qa.a: They could keep a box of safe odds and ends for him and ask, "What else could this be?" 🙂

qa.q: How does Afreen see Bhupen's play?
qa.a: Afreen watches with amused admiration, unsure where the ideas come from but impressed that they never run out.

grounding: Illustrates a young child inventing many uses for leftover festival bamboo and straw.

passage: On Three Kings' Day, the park in Madrid was full of children with new toys. Clara and Pablo played tag round the frozen fountain. Pablo ran fast, but at each corner he slowed and leaned in so he wouldn't slip on the ice. When he caught Clara, he grabbed her in a tight hug. "Stop, too squeezy!" she said. Pablo let go at once and stepped back. "Sorry. Tag with one finger?" Clara grinned. "One finger. Go!" This time he tapped her shoulder lightly and ran.

qa.q: What did Clara say when Pablo hugged her?
qa.a: "Stop, too squeezy!"

qa.q: Why did Pablo let go at once and step back?
qa.a: He wanted Clara to feel comfortable and seemed a little embarrassed that his hug had been too tight.

qa.q: What could an adult say to encourage how Pablo handled it?
qa.a: They could say, "You listened when Clara said stop, and you found a new way to play."

qa.q: How does Clara feel when Pablo suggests "one finger"?
qa.a: Clara feels respected and happy to keep playing, since her "stop" was heard straight away. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child keeping his balance on ice during a winter game and respecting a friend's body boundary.

passage: On Pola morning in their village near Wardha, everyone was decorating the bullocks. For days Vasudha had tried to tie the brass bell on Shyam the bullock's neck rope, and each time the knot slipped. Today she pulled the ends tight, tugged, and the bell held. She stepped back, chin up, and rang it twice. "I did it myself!" Her cousin Bhupen looked over from painting the horns. "Not bad, Vasu." She walked Shyam to the gate so everyone passing could hear the bell.

qa.q: What had Vasudha tried to tie on Shyam's neck rope?
qa.a: She had tried to tie the brass bell.

qa.q: What does Vasudha walking to the gate suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels proud of her knot and wants others to notice it.

qa.q: How could her family support her pride in a healthy way?
qa.a: They could notice her effort, like "You kept trying for days", rather than just calling her clever.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Vasudha's achievement?
qa.a: Bhupen treats it lightly with "Not bad, Vasu", which sounds like a cousin's teasing but still approving.

grounding: Shows a young child standing taller with satisfaction after finally mastering a task during a village festival.

passage:
Teacher's note, Annual Day rehearsal, December
During the winter-song rehearsal, Eshaan forgot his two lines. A few children giggled. He dropped his head, pulled his jumper over his face and whispered, "I'm a bad boy. I can't do anything." He wouldn't come out from behind the curtain. His friend Devika sat beside him and said, "I forgot mine yesterday." I told him forgetting is something everyone does, not something he is. We practised the lines quietly, just the three of us. I'll call his parents tonight so they can reassure him too.

qa.q: What did Eshaan pull over his face?
qa.a: He pulled his jumper over his face.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he said, "I'm a bad boy"?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, as if forgetting the lines meant he himself was bad, not just that he had made a mistake.

qa.q: What could Eshaan's parents say tonight?
qa.a: They could remind him that everyone forgets things and that they love him just the same, then practise the lines together for fun.

qa.q: How does Devika help Eshaan feel less alone?
qa.a: By saying "I forgot mine yesterday", Devika shows Eshaan that it happens to others too.

grounding: Illustrates a young child feeling bad about himself after failing at a rehearsal, and a teacher separating the mistake from the child.

passage: On Eid morning in their small town, Mehak showed off her new green glass bangles. Rehana wanted a turn and tugged at them. One snapped and fell in pieces on the courtyard floor. Mehak cried. Rehana stood very still, her face hot. Then she hid behind the water drum. After a while she came out holding her own red bangle and pushed it into Mehak's hand. "I pulled. I'm sorry. You have mine." Khala swept up the glass and hugged them both.

qa.q: What colour were Mehak's new bangles?
qa.a: They were green glass bangles.

qa.q: Why did Rehana hide behind the water drum?
qa.a: She felt guilty and upset about breaking Mehak's bangle and wasn't ready to face her yet.

qa.q: What did Rehana's apology get right?
qa.a: She named exactly what she did ("I pulled"), said sorry, and tried to make up for it by giving her own bangle.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel when Rehana offers her own bangle?
qa.a: Mehak would likely feel comforted, seeing that Rehana is truly sorry and cares about her. 🤍

grounding: Shows a young child feeling remorse for breaking a cousin's bangle and trying to make amends.

passage: At the Lunar New Year dinner in Vancouver, Grandma said, "Bao, say your new year wish for everyone!" Twelve faces turned toward him. Someone lifted a phone to film. Bao's cheeks went pink. He slid off his chair and pressed his face into his cousin Ada's sleeve. "Too many people," he mumbled. Ada leaned down. "Want to whisper it to me, and I'll say it?" He nodded and whispered. Ada announced, "Bao wishes everyone lots of dumplings!" Everyone cheered, and Bao peeked out, smiling.

qa.q: How many faces turned toward Bao?
qa.a: Twelve faces turned toward him.

qa.q: What do Bao's pink cheeks and hidden face suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone watching him at once.

qa.q: How could Grandma ask next time so Bao feels less on the spot?
qa.a: She could ask him quietly first, or let him share his wish with just one person.

qa.q: What is it like for Ada to help Bao?
qa.a: Ada seems protective and kind, finding a way for Bao to join in without facing all the attention.

grounding: Illustrates a young child's sudden self-consciousness when a whole family dinner table turns to watch him.

passage: On a hot January afternoon at a beach near Sydney, Rosa watched a wave wash away her friend Mei's sandcastle. Mei sat down in the wet sand and cried. Rosa stopped digging. Her mouth turned down, and she stood very still with her spade hanging from her hand. "Mei's castle is gone," she told her dad in a small voice, eyes filling. "She's sad." Her dad crouched beside her. "You're sad for her too, aren't you?" Rosa nodded and looked back at Mei.

qa.q: What washed away Mei's sandcastle?
qa.a: A wave washed it away.

qa.q: What does Rosa's small voice and filling eyes suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt sad and sorry for Mei, sharing a little of her friend's upset.

qa.q: What could Rosa's dad suggest next?
qa.a: He could ask Rosa if she'd like to sit with Mei, or help build a new castle further from the waves.

qa.q: What would change for Mei if Rosa went over to sit beside her?
qa.a: Mei might feel less alone and comforted, knowing her friend noticed and cared.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling sorrow on seeing a friend cry over a lost sandcastle in the southern summer.

passage: During the long rains in Nairobi, the school courtyard was slippery. Abebe skidded and landed hard on his knee. He held it and rocked, crying. Kofi ran over and crouched beside him. He looked at the knee, then patted Abebe's back, round and round, the way his mum did for him. "It's okay, it's okay." Then he peeled the dinosaur sticker off his own lunchbox and stuck it on Abebe's shirt. "For brave." He stayed next to him until the teacher came with the first-aid box.

qa.q: What did Kofi stick on Abebe's shirt?
qa.a: He stuck the dinosaur sticker from his own lunchbox on Abebe's shirt.

qa.q: Why did Kofi pat Abebe's back round and round?
qa.a: He was worried about Abebe and wanted to comfort him, the way his mum comforts him.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond to Kofi's kindness?
qa.a: After caring for the knee, the teacher could thank Kofi for staying with Abebe until help came.

qa.q: What is it like for Abebe to have Kofi beside him?
qa.a: Abebe, in pain, likely feels less frightened and alone with a friend patting his back.

grounding: Illustrates a young child noticing a friend's pain and trying simple ways to comfort him.

passage: At the community centre's Holi party, the children played musical chairs. When the music stopped, Sarita slid onto the last chair and Binita was out. Binita stamped her foot, and her lip wobbled. She marched to the corner, squeezed her fists, then sat hugging her knees and blowing slow breaths, like blowing out birthday candles. Sarita called, "Binita, come be the music person!" After a minute, Binita wiped her eyes, walked over, and pressed play. By the next round she was grinning as she stopped the music.

qa.q: Who got the last chair?
qa.a: Sarita slid onto the last chair.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and angry at being out of the game.

qa.q: What helped Binita calm down, and what could an adult add?
qa.a: Slow breaths and a little time alone helped; an adult could quietly name her feeling and praise her for coming back. 👍

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when Binita comes over to press play?
qa.a: Sarita is probably relieved and pleased to have Binita back in the game.

grounding: Shows a young child recovering from losing a party game by calming herself instead of melting down.
